summary: Defines a minimal set of requirements that an instant messaging and presence protocol must meet. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2779 sets minimum requirements for protocols that carry instant messages and presence information, such as whether someone is online. It describes what a protocol should support so independently built services can work together, but it does not define a protocol.

subtitle: The minimum requirements for interoperable instant messaging and presence protocols.

tldr.problem: Instant messaging and presence services used separate vendor protocols that did not interoperate, preventing independently developed applications from working together.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists shared, service-specific, and security requirements for a standard protocol, including naming, scale, access control, message formats, delivery, and privacy.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2779 is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol specification. It states the minimum conditions that a proposed instant messaging and presence protocol must meet.

facts.label: Scale design goal
facts.value: Millions of entities per domain and millions of domains

today: RFC 2779 is an Informational memo. It sets protocol requirements and does not define an instant messaging or presence protocol.

sections.title: What Presence and Messaging Mean
sections.content:
Presence lets a user find, retrieve, and subscribe to changes in another user's information, such as online or offline status. Instant messaging sends short messages intended for immediate delivery to online users. The goal of the IMPP Working Group was a standard protocol so independently developed applications could interoperate across the Internet.

The memo defines terms for the people and services involved, including presentity, watcher, subscriber, notification, and instant inbox. In this document, MUST means a proposed solution has to meet a requirement, while SHOULD means a proposed solution may choose not to meet it; the RFC notes that this differs from RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence reports information such as whether a person is online, and messaging carries short messages between users. This memo defines shared terms and explains how it uses MUST and SHOULD.

sections.title: Requirements Shared by Both Services
sections.content:
The protocol must work in settings with high delay, low bandwidth, intermittent connections, limited computing power, and small displays. It must allow presence and messaging services to exist independently and must let entities in separate domains interoperate without having known one another beforehand.

The design goals include millions of entities within one domain and millions of domains. People controlling a presentity or instant inbox must be able to decide who can see status, subscribe, send messages, or read messages. The protocol must allow direct communication and communication through proxies, and give administrators ways to filter it at common firewalls.
sections.plainLanguage: The services must work on constrained devices and across many independently managed domains. Each person or organization must control who can see status information and who can send or read messages.

sections.title: Presence and Message Formats
sections.content:
All entities must support a common base format for presence information. It must identify the presentity, carry contact information when applicable, and allow extensions without breaking the base fields. A service must allow fetching or subscribing even when the presentity is out of contact, and must notify subscribers of changes unless access rules prevent it.

Instant messages need a common base format that identifies the sender and intended recipient and includes a return address. The format must allow different payload encodings, and should be based on MIME. The sender must be able to learn whether delivery succeeded or why it failed. In systems that support both services, presence information must represent OPEN and CLOSED status.
sections.plainLanguage: Different services need common ways to describe status and messages. A message identifies its sender and recipient, provides a reply address, and lets the sender learn whether delivery succeeded.

sections.title: Security, Privacy and User Control
sections.content:
The requirements let a presentity owner accept, refuse, cancel, or quietly block subscriptions. They also require ways to identify and authenticate subscribers, prevent unauthorized subscription changes, and avoid requiring either side to reveal its IP address to the other.

Notifications and instant messages must be protected against unwanted reading and tampering, and recipients need ways to verify who sent them. A delivered instant message must reach the recipient only once, while the sender must receive confirmation of non-delivery. The protocol must allow digital signatures using existing standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Users control who follows their status and who can send messages. The protocol must provide ways to protect messages from reading or changes and to check who sent them.

sections.title: A Set of Requirements, Not a Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 2779 describes the minimum requirements for a future instant messaging and presence protocol. It covers the goals and constraints that a protocol design must address, including scale, access control, message handling, and security.

The document does not specify message exchanges or a protocol implementation. It is an Informational memo that serves as a requirements list.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a checklist for protocol designers, not a protocol that services can implement. It describes the required behavior without defining how to encode or exchange messages.
